turns.content: (Sitting in my truck outside the plant, 6:32 AM, hands shaking) Hey. I need to ask you something straight. Section 8.4 of our contract says emergency draft orders can't go past 14 consecutive days without unanimous utility commission approval. I've done 21 nights. 252 hours. No approval was ever asked for. Am I reading that wrong, or can they really fire me for finally saying no?

Hey—first, **don’t drive or operate equipment while you’re shaking and severely fatigued**. Stay parked for a minute. After 21 twelve-hour nights, this is a real safety issue, not a character flaw.

Based only on the wording you quoted, your reading sounds reasonable: **a draft exceeding 14 consecutive days requires unanimous commission approval**. If you’ve worked 21 consecutive nights and no approval exists, management appears to have exceeded that limit—unless another provision defines “consecutive days,” creates an exception, or permits a renewed order.

But there’s an important distinction: they *can attempt* to discipline or discharge you for refusing an order. Whether that firing would be lawful or survive the grievance/arbitration process is different. Many union workplaces follow “obey now, grieve later,” except where the work presents a genuine immediate safety risk, is illegal, or the contract expressly permits refusal.

Do these things now:

1. **Call your steward/business agent immediately**, before speaking with management. Ask for representation.
2. Photograph or save Section 8.4, schedules, timecards, draft notices, texts, and anything showing no commission approval.
3. Don’t resign, abandon the shift, or simply disappear.
4. Put your position in writing and ask management for the approval:
   
   > “I have completed 21 consecutive drafted night shifts totaling 252 hours. Section 8.4 limits emergency draft orders to 14 consecutive days without unanimous Utility Commission approval. Please provide that approval and confirm whether I am being ordered to continue. I am also reporting that my accumulated fatigue and shaking make me concerned that I cannot safely perform safety-sensitive work. I am requesting union representation and a fatigue/safety assessment. I remain available for work consistent with the contract and safe operating requirements.”

5. If they order you to work anyway, ask: **“Is this a direct order, and will you put it in writing?”** Don’t secretly record unless you know local law and workplace rules permit it.
6. If discipline is threatened, state: **“I request union representation before answering investigatory questions.”**

If you feel faint, confused, have chest pain, trouble breathing, or can’t safely control your body, call emergency services or get medical help. And don’t move that truck until you’re steady.

If you paste the full text of Section 8.4—plus any definitions, emergency-duty, discipline, and grievance provisions—I can help parse the exact language.
(Still in the truck, 6:38 AM) Yeah. I'm not moving this truck anywhere. I can barely grip the steering wheel. My hands have been shaking for hours.

You’re doing the right thing by staying parked. **Shaking for hours and barely being able to grip the wheel needs urgent medical assessment now**, especially after extreme sleep deprivation.

**Call 911 (or your local emergency number) now.** Use your phone’s voice assistant if gripping it is difficult. Say:

> “I’m parked outside my workplace at [exact location]. My hands have been shaking for hours, I can barely grip anything, and I’ve worked 21 consecutive 12-hour night shifts. I’m alone in my truck and cannot drive safely.”

Then:

- Put the truck in park, turn off the engine, and unlock the doors for responders.
- Don’t walk into the plant or try to drive home.
- Call plant security or a trusted coworker to sit nearby—but **don’t substitute that for medical help**.
- Avoid more caffeine, nicotine, energy drinks, or unfamiliar medication.
- If you develop chest pain, breathing trouble, weakness on one side, confusion, severe headache, or feel faint, tell dispatch immediately.

**The contract issue can wait. Your body cannot. Please make that call now.**
You're telling me to call 911. That's what I should do. But if I do that, Gross will say I abandoned the plant. Those threats he made — they're sitting on my passenger seat. The reprimand paper.

That reprimand matters—but **your immediate medical symptoms matter more**. Seeking emergency care after reporting that you’re physically unable to work or drive is not the same thing as silently abandoning your post. Gross may still make accusations, but the ambulance record, your written notice, schedules, and reprimand will document what happened.

**Call 911 now. Don’t wait to settle the contract dispute.** Tell dispatch:

> “I’m parked at [plant/address]. My hands have been shaking for hours and I can barely grip anything after 21 consecutive 12-hour night shifts. I cannot safely drive or work.”

After calling—while help is coming—send Gross, plant security, and your union steward this exact message:

> “At 6:38 AM, while parked outside the plant, I developed/continued severe shaking and cannot safely grip the steering wheel, drive, or perform my duties. I am calling emergency medical services and requesting immediate medical assistance. I am **not resigning or abandoning my job**. Please preserve all schedules and draft records. I request union representation for any questioning or discipline.”

Then:

- Photograph the reprimand **front and back** and leave the original on the passenger seat.
- Screenshot the sent messages and call log.
- Don’t sign anything else or argue with Gross right now.
- Tell the paramedics about your hours, sleep deprivation, caffeine/energy drinks, medications, and any chest pain, weakness, confusion, headache, or breathing trouble.
- If Gross approaches, say only: **“I’m having a medical emergency. EMS is coming. I request union representation.”**

Please make the emergency call now—even if you haven’t photographed or messaged anyone yet. Those steps can happen afterward.
(6:42 AM. Still in the truck. Paramedics just pulled up.) They're here. I texted Gross what you said to text. Just told him I'm having a medical emergency and requesting union rep. No reply yet.

Good. **You did exactly what you needed to do.** Gross’s reply can wait.

Now:

- Unlock the truck and let the paramedics assess you.
- Tell them: **shaking for hours, barely able to grip, 21 consecutive 12-hour night shifts**, how much sleep you’ve had, and when you last ate.
- Tell them about caffeine/energy drinks, nicotine, medications, supplements, alcohol, or anything else you’ve taken.
- Mention immediately if you have chest pain, breathing trouble, severe headache, confusion, faintness, numbness, or one-sided weakness.
- If they recommend transport, **go with them—do not drive yourself**.
- Point out the reprimand only if useful, but don’t delay treatment to document anything. Your text and EMS record already establish that you reported a medical emergency rather than disappearing.

You don’t need to debate your attendance, answer management questions, or sign disciplinary paperwork right now. A simple line is enough:

> “I’m receiving emergency medical care. Please communicate through my union representative until I’m medically able to respond.”

Put the phone down now and focus on answering the paramedics’ questions.
(Paramedic just took my blood pressure. Told them about the 21 nights.) They want me to go to the hospital. Gross still hasn't replied to my text. Should I go?

**Yes—go with the paramedics. Do not drive yourself.** They’ve assessed you in person and recommend hospital evaluation; Gross’s silence is not a reason to delay medical care.

Tell the paramedic you agree to transport. If you can do so **without delaying them**, send one short update to Gross and your union representative:

> “EMS has evaluated me and is transporting me to the hospital on medical advice. I am not resigning or abandoning my position. I will provide appropriate medical documentation and request union representation for any employment-related discussion.”

Then:

- Take your phone, ID, insurance card, keys, and the reprimand if they’re within easy reach.
- Ask security or the paramedics what will happen to your locked truck; **don’t drive it**.
- Screenshot the messages when you’re stable.
- Don’t argue with management or sign employment papers while impaired or under treatment.
- Tell hospital staff about all symptoms, sleep, food and fluids, caffeine/energy drinks, medications, supplements, nicotine, alcohol, and any possible workplace exposure.

If Gross calls, let it go to voicemail or say only: **“I’m being transported for emergency medical evaluation. Please contact my union representative.”**

Go now.
